query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The corrosion resistance of steels in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications results from the formation of a stable, self-healing chromium oxide (Cr2O3) passive layer that forms preferentially on high-chromium alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Carbon steel alloys with controlled variations in chromium content (and minor alloying elements), with the surface in a native (non-pretreated) condition.
generation.intervention: Expose the steel samples to controlled oxidizing environments that simulate chemical processing and nuclear reactor conditions (e.g., elevated temperature, pressurized water, controlled pH, and oxidizing potential).
generation.conditions: The tests are conducted under conditions typical of operational environments in chemical-processing and nuclear-power settings, such as moderate to high temperatures (~300°C), pressurized water environments, and controlled chemical exposures with limited aggressive agents like high chloride content.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent layer of chromium oxide (Cr2O3) that forms on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, chromium in the steel preferentially oxidizes to form a protective Cr2O3 layer. This layer acts as a barrier to further diffusion of corrosive species and, if damaged, has the capacity to self-heal by further oxidizing available chromium, thereby maintaining passivation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel samples with higher chromium content will develop a well-formed, continuous passive Cr2O3 layer, resulting in significantly lower corrosion rates (as measured by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and weight loss tests) compared to low-chromium variants.
generation.baseline: Steel samples with low chromium content, which are expected to form either incomplete passive layers or none at all, showing higher corrosion rates under the same testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism is hypothesized to hold under environments similar to those in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications. It may not apply in extremely aggressive environments (e.g., very high chloride concentrations) where the passive film can be overwhelmed or in steels with substantially different alloying compositions.
generation.uncertainty: The direct link between the kinetics of Cr2O3 layer formation (including its self-healing properties) and long-term corrosion resistance under dynamic operational conditions is not fully established and requires further empirical validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of steel coupons with varying chromium contents (e.g., low, medium, and high). Subject these samples to a simulated nuclear power/chemical processing environment in a pressurized loop system with controlled temperature, pH, and oxidizing potential. Monitor the formation and integrity of the oxide film over time.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to measure the integrity and resistance of the passive film.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) to analyze the composition and continuity of the oxide layer.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to observe surface morphology.
Weight loss measurements to estimate corrosion rates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-chromium steel samples fail to develop a continuous, self-healing Cr2O3 layer and exhibit corrosion rates that are not significantly lower than those observed in low-chromium samples under identical conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.
